How harbor tides work

Tides are the regular rise and fall of sea levels caused by the gravitational pull of the moon and the sun. Coastal harbors experience two high tides and two low tides on most days, although the exact timing shifts by about fifty minutes each day.

Engineers who design harbors must account for the tidal range, because ships need enough depth at the quay during low water. In some bays the difference between high and low water exceeds ten meters, which changes the way docks and locks are built.

Local authorities publish tide tables every year. Sailors compare these tables with live gauge readings, since strong winds and atmospheric pressure can raise or lower the water level by several tens of centimeters.
